hints: Compare the formulae of $\text{NH}_{3}$ on the left and $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ on the right of the equation and identify what small particle has been gained during the change.
walkthrough:
Recall what makes a Bronsted-Lowry base**
Think of a Bronsted-Lowry base simply as a proton acceptor. A proton here means a hydrogen ion, $\text{H}^{+}$. If a species gains $\text{H}^{+}$ in a reaction, it is acting as the base.

Spot the change from ammonia to ammonium**
Look at the equation. $\text{NH}_{3}$ becomes $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ in $\text{NH}_{4}\text{NO}_{3}$. The nitrogen has gained one hydrogen and one positive charge, which is exactly gain of $\text{H}^{+}$: $$\text{NH}_{3} + \text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{NH}_{4}^{+}$$ So ammonia is the proton acceptor, the Bronsted-Lowry base.
Final answer: Ammonia accepts a proton, $\text{H}^{+}$, to form $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$.

hints: Think about which product contains nitrogen and why farmers want to supply nitrogen to growing plants.
Think about soil acidity and which product contains carbonate that can react with $\text{H}^{+}$ in the soil to raise pH.
walkthrough:
Link ammonium nitrate to plant nutrition**
Plants need nitrogen to make proteins and grow well. $\text{NH}_{4}\text{NO}_{3}$ supplies nitrogen in two useful forms, ammonium and nitrate, so the mixture acts as a fertiliser that adds nutrients to the soil.

Link calcium carbonate to soil pH**
Many soils are too acidic for good growth. $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ is a base that reacts with and neutralises excess soil acid, raising the soil pH toward neutral. This improves conditions for plants and for nutrient uptake.

Final answer: 1. Acts as a fertiliser, provides nitrogen / nutrients for plant growth.
2. Neutralises acidic soil / increases pH of acidic soil.

hints: For each central atom, count the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs: $\text{CO}_{2}$ has 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs, $\text{NH}_{3}$ has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs.

Remember that lone pair to lone pair repulsion is greater than lone pair to bonding pair repulsion, which is greater than bonding pair to bonding pair repulsion, so each extra lone pair squeezes the bond angle smaller.
Link the electron pair counts to the standard VSEPR outcomes, starting from $180^{\circ}$ for two charge centres and from $109.5^{\circ}$ for four charge centres.
walkthrough:
Use electron pairs to predict shape**
Picture the central atom and count regions of electrons. In $\text{CO}_{2}$, carbon has 2 double bonds and no lone pairs, so the two bonding regions push as far apart as possible. In $\text{NH}_{3}$, nitrogen has 3 bonds plus 1 lone pair, four regions in total. In $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, oxygen has 2 bonds plus 2 lone pairs, also four regions in total.

Explain $\text{CO}_{2}$ as linear**
With only two electron regions and no lone pairs on carbon, repulsion is minimised when they are opposite each other. That gives a linear molecule with bond angle: $$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O} \quad 180^{\circ}$$

Explain $\text{NH}_{3}$ as pyramidal**
Four electron pairs arrange tetrahedrally, but only three are bonds. The lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs and squeezes the $\text{H-N-H}$ angle down from $109.5^{\circ}$ to about $107^{\circ}$. With the lone pair on top, the three H atoms form a trigonal pyramid.

Explain $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ as bent**
Here there are two lone pairs, which repel even more strongly. They squeeze the $\text{H-O-H}$ angle down further to $104.5^{\circ}$. The molecule is described as bent, V-shaped or non-linear.

Final answer: $\text{CO}_{2}$: linear, $180^{\circ}$
$\text{NH}_{3}$: pyramidal, $107^{\circ}$
$\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$: bent / non-linear / V-shaped, $104.5^{\circ}$
